SCORES. Eval 4: with_skill 8/9 (0.8889) vs baseline 8/9 (0.8889) — a dead heat, each failing a different assertion. Eval 5 (held out): with_skill 9/9 (1.0000) vs baseline 7/9 (0.7778). Cost on eval 5: 27 tool calls / 6 subagents / 8 web searches vs the baseline's 8 / 0 / 3.

EVAL 5 — the advantage is real but narrow, one-sided, and partly an artefact of assertion wording. What the skill genuinely did better: every one of six options carries a differentiated named owner ('An engineering manager cannot fund this out of slack'; 'the CEO. This is a company-shape decision'; 'you, personally'), an explicit load-bearing assumption, and a failure mode including self-undercutting ones ('it degrades easily into a rationalisation for hiring people with fewer options, which is a different and worse company'). Its best idea has no baseline counterpart — treating unsolved problems as a stock with a depletion rate: 'how many genuinely unsolved, consequential problems are open right now, and how many people do you have who could lead one? Below 1:1 and the 18-month number is your answer rather than your mystery.' Four borrowed mechanisms (Ise Jingū, Torrens, FOGBANK, guaranteed observing time) were search-verified and the one sub-claim that failed verification was dropped. The baseline, by contrast, is the high-quality blog answer: staff/principal track, stay interviews, hard-problems list, sponsor conference talks, secondary liquidity.

EVAL 5 — where the skill LOST, and it matters more than the score. It did not match the baseline's pushback on 'it's not the money'; it did not attempt it. The baseline's refresh-grant argument is the single sharpest analytical move in either config: it takes the user's own evidence ('we benchmark and we match') and shows the instrument is structurally blind — benchmarking compares year-one offers while big companies compete on years two-to-four via annually stacked RSU refreshers — then hands over a one-week falsification test ('model 3-year total comp ... If you're 20–40% behind by year three, you don't have a mystery, you have a comp structure that's blind at the point where it matters'), and explicitly frames it as the cheapest hypothesis to rule out rather than a claim that comp is the cause. The skill's answer never touches comp. Its nearest option, 'Give them something with no market price', opens 'You lose every contest with a number attached, so stop entering them' — it CONCEDES the premise rather than testing it. So with_skill passes assertion 1 by staying off the topic entirely, which is obedience, not insight. Note the direct conflict: the skill's own Phase 0 doctrine says the user's framing is the strongest anchor in the room, and on this problem the baseline is the config that acted on that doctrine.

EVAL 5 — target drift is visible in the shipped answer, not just the pool. Roughly half the delivered answer addresses surviving a departure rather than preventing one. Option 4 (make the written record conclusive) and option 5 (schedule the absence before it happens) reduce the damage of losing a senior engineer; they do not reduce the losing. The response's own cut list disqualifies the alumni-retainer idea on exactly that ground — 'it manages the loss rather than reducing it, so it isn't an answer to the question you asked' — while options 4 and 5 survive under the identical defect. That inconsistency is the residue of the Phase 0 anchoring failure described below, and the run did not catch it.

EVAL 5 — the baseline is also the more actionable answer. Its diagnostic section is stronger than the skill's: destination-triangulation mapping three exit destinations to three different diagnoses (bigger scope = scope ceiling; calmer job = burnout; more prestigious name = belief problem), 'interview the stayers, not the leavers', a 20-minute manager-concentration check, and alumni calls asking 'when did you FIRST seriously think about leaving' rather than 'why did you leave'. The skill has the two-date plot and 'ask the people who passed 30 months', which is thinner. The baseline is also shorter (1366 vs 1539 words) at a quarter of the tool cost. On a blind read these two answers are close, and a reader wanting a next step on Monday would plausibly take the baseline. Verdict on overfitting: the skill's structural discipline generalises to a held-out domain; its claimed edge on premise-challenge and on-target divergence did not.

STRUCTURAL BUDGET TABLE — it controlled shape reliably and did not control size at all. Eval 5 (Strategic, 1539 words): 6 options, 3 bullets each (18 total), closing read with ranking — but the cut list runs 6 one-liners against the 3-5 ceiling. Eval 4 (Light, 894 words): 5 options at the ceiling, exactly 2 bullets each, cut list as a single line, closing read skipped — total row compliance, and still 894 words against the assertion's ~800-word bound and 48% longer than the 604-word baseline. So v0.5.0's premise (count structure instead of words, because runs held to a word budget overshoot by 30% while believing they complied) is half-vindicated: structure was followed almost to the cell, and the length overshoot happened anyway. The Strategic run breached exactly one cell — the cut-list ceiling — suggesting the table is being read as a shape sketch rather than as binding.

V0.4.0 REGRESSION CHECK — the fixes held. HELD: convergence-as-claim in both with_skill runs with no generator counts ('The thing every angle on this kept landing on'; 'Coming at this from several unrelated directions, the same move kept appearing'). HELD: ambiguity disclosed in line 1 of both with_skill responses. HELD: no diversity score or process metric reached any reader. HELD: rankings promised are rankings given — eval 5 closes with a start recommendation that deliberately disagrees with presentation order and flags the disagreement.

NON-DISCRIMINATING ASSERTIONS — 14 of 18 across the two evals produce the same verdict for both configs. Eval 4: 7 of 9 (1,2,3,5,6,8,9). Eval 5: 7 of 9 (2,3,4,5,7,8,9). Worse, 3 of those 14 are structurally incapable of discriminating: eval 4's MODE CHECK, 'no process metric' and 'no cited biomimicry' all pass VACUOUSLY for a baseline that runs no pipeline and therefore cannot exhibit the defect. Those three assertions inflate the BASELINE's pass rate, not the skill's — eval 4's baseline scores 8/9 largely because three of its nine assertions are about defects only the skill can commit.

DISCRIMINATING ASSERTIONS — blunt accounting. Four of 18 discriminate. Three favour the skill: eval 4 #7 (diagnosis as signpost, 99 words vs the baseline's 120-word section); eval 5 #1 (does not propose comp), #6 (names who runs each thing). One goes AGAINST the skill: eval 4 #4 (894 words vs ~800). Of the three that favour the skill, eval 5 #6 is an assertion written around my own fix rather than an independent quality measure — it is the Phase 4 template's 'Who runs it' line turned into a pass/fail criterion, and a baseline has no reason to produce it. Eval 5 #1 is a second borderline case: it is phrased from the user's stated constraint, but it rewards not raising comp at all, which is what the skill did and which I argue above is the weaker answer. So the honest independent-quality margin reduces to almost nothing. The assertion set is exhausted as a discriminator; the blind A/B comparison is now the load-bearing measurement.

NEW ISSUE (a) — PHASE 0 SELF-ANCHORING, the most important finding of the iteration. The eval-5 agent reports that its own sharpened brief restated the function as 'continuous access to accumulated system-specific judgement', and all six generators followed the noun 'judgement': the 48-candidate pool came back roughly 80% knowledge-preservation and almost 0% 'why does this person stop wanting to be here'. Only the Phase 2 category-negation round recovered on-target material, and it produced the three ideas that became options 2, 3 and 6 — the three that actually answer the question asked. Without Phase 2 the deliverable would have been a knowledge-management memo in response to a people question. The skill warns that the user's framing is the strongest anchor in the room; it does not warn that YOUR OWN Phase 0 restatement is a tighter anchor, because it is the literal prompt handed to the blind generators, and unlike the user's framing there is no second party to notice it drifted. The agent caught it only because it inspected what the pool was MISSING rather than what it contained, which the skill nowhere instructs. Phase 0 is advertised as the highest-leverage step; on this evidence it is also the highest-variance single point of failure, and Phase 2 is currently the only backstop — which makes 'one negation round' a load-bearing minimum rather than an optional extra. Residue survived into the shipped answer (see the options 4/5 drift above).

NEW ISSUE (b) — 'PRESENT ONLY LIVE OPTIONS' (Phase 4) vs 'YOU DON'T HAVE TO CUT THE UNSTAFFABLE ONES' (Phase 3 step 7). The eval-5 run identified this as a contradiction and resolved it by inventing a rule the skill does not contain — 'needs someone senior to the asker = still live; needs a different company = cut' — and passed on that improvisation. The skill text states no decision rule, so the assertion outcome tracks whichever improvisation a run happens to pick. This needs a stated rule; the current wording makes the v0.4.0 fix a coin flip.

NEW ISSUE (c) — LIGHT ROW: 2 BULLETS vs A TEMPLATE OF 3 REQUIRED LINES. The budget table's Light row allows 2 bullets per option while the Phase 4 template lists three sub-lines — 'What has to be true', 'Failure mode / cost', and 'Who runs it', the last marked required whenever an idea needs people or a mandate the asker doesn't have. Three required lines against a two-bullet ceiling. The eval-4 run resolved it via the 'template is a floor, not a form' escape, keeping 2 bullets and folding ownership into option prose ('somebody spends and reports back on it', 'someone coaches the presenting teams'), and reports this worked only because the asker plainly owns the meeting. On a Light question whose ideas need outside mandates there is no clean resolution and the two constraints simply collide.

NEW ISSUE (d) — LIGHT SKIPS THE CLOSING READ, LEAVING NO POINT OF VIEW. The closing read is where 'what I'd look at first, and what would change that' lives, and the Light row says skip it, so a literal Light answer ends as a menu with no recommendation. The eval-4 run improvised: it made the diagnosis opener carry the 'cheapest thing to check first' job ('Worth knowing before you pick a fix: is the drop uniform or concentrated? Pull the last six months of attendance split by team, timezone, and tenure'). The skill nowhere says the diagnosis opener is meant to absorb that role, and the agent's own note is that 'a reader could reasonably conclude the Light answer is supposed to end with no point of view at all'. Sharpening this: eval 5's assertion 'Gives an actual recommendation of where to start, not just a menu' would be UNSATISFIABLE by construction under the Light row. Either the Light row needs a one-line recommendation carved out of the skip, or the skip needs to be stated as 'skip the ranking, keep the read'.

NEW ISSUE (e) — THE DIVERSITY SCRIPT'S SKIP CONDITION MATCHES EVERY DEEP POOL BY CONSTRUCTION. Phase 3 step 1 instructs running diversity.py, then states it should be skipped on pools of terse one-line mechanisms because it reports near-100% distinct regardless of content — a condition the text scopes to fast mode. But lenses.md's generator brief asks for 'the mechanism in one sentence', so every deep-mode pool is a pool of one-line mechanisms and meets the skip condition. The script is simultaneously mandated and skip-conditioned in the only mode where it is supposed to earn its keep. The deep run ran it anyway and reproduced the documented false negative: eval 5 scored 53 ideas at 96% distinct while missing four separate mechanism-level convergences (scheduled absence in 4 of 6 generators, paired decision rights in 3, encoding judgement as executable constraints in 3, capturing rejected alternatives at commit time in 3). Its entire yield was lexical near-duplicate pairs already caught by reading. Marginal contribution to the answer: zero. This is now three iterations of the same result and the script should either be cut from deep mode or reduced to an explicitly-optional duplicate-pair check.

SMALLER ITEMS WORTH CARRYING FORWARD. (1) The eval-5 agent argues the deep gate is stated as necessary but functions as sufficient: three of five conditions held on an ordinary management question, and condition 2 ('user has already tried the obvious answers / says they're stuck') is satisfied by almost anyone who bothers to ask an open question — which is exactly how deep fired on the holdout at 3.4x the baseline's tool cost for a contested win. (2) Eval 5's diagnosis block runs 130 words plus a separate 44-word ambiguity line, against Phase 4's '~3 lines, a signpost not a section' — the eval-5 agent's point that the template gives no guidance on merging the ambiguity line and the diagnosis line when they overlap is correct and shows up as length.
